title: Bachelet Quits UN Race After Support Collapses in Straw Poll
summary:
For 80 years, the United Nations has had 80 years of male leaders. Michelle Bachelet, the former president of Chile, wanted to be the first woman to break that streak. On Saturday, she ended her bid.

Bachelet, 74, announced the decision in a video posted on Instagram. "Today I announced that I have decided not to continue with my candidacy for the position of Secretary-General of the United Nations," she said. She added that she did not regret "having taken on this great challenge," even if "the time was not right."

The timing was no accident. On Friday, the UN Security Council released its third informal straw poll — a kind of secret practice vote that lets countries signal support without a formal commitment. Bachelet received just one "encourage" vote, 11 "discourage" votes and three "no opinion" votes. In July she had six encouraging votes; in August, only two. Her support was shrinking fast.

The same poll put Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan, who leads the UN's Trade and Development body, in front with nine encouraging votes. Guyana's Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett followed with eight. Other candidates still running include Rafael Grossi of the International Atomic Energy Agency, former Senegalese President Macky Sall, and Ecuadorian diplomat Maria Fernanda Espinosa.

The rules are tough. To be recommended by the Security Council, a candidate needs at least nine of its 15 members to vote in favour — and must avoid a veto from any of the five permanent members: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. Then the General Assembly holds a final vote.

Bachelet was nominated by Chile in February, with backing from Brazil and Mexico. Only one Latin American, Peru's Javier Perez de Cuellar, has ever held the UN's top job, and an unofficial rotation had put Latin America in line this cycle.

Whoever replaces Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on December 31, inherits a difficult job. Guterres warned earlier this year that the UN faced "imminent financial collapse," with $1.57bn in unpaid dues by the end of 2025. He also said geopolitical divides among major powers have left the body deadlocked on Gaza, Ukraine and other crises. World leaders gather in New York next week for the General Assembly's annual high-level session, opening Tuesday under the theme "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation."
why_it_matters: Who leads the UN shapes how the world answers wars, famines and climate disasters, yet the choice is effectively made by five veto-wielding powers — raising hard questions about legitimacy, gender and whether global institutions can still act in a deeply divided world.

background_read: The United Nations (founded in 1945 after the Second World War, and now a forum where almost every country meets to discuss peace, aid and international law) has had nine Secretaries-General, and all of them have been men.

The job is never openly contested in a worldwide vote: the Security Council — whose five permanent members are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — recommends a single name behind closed doors, and the 193-member General Assembly then approves it. That makes any one of the five vetoes decisive.

An informal tradition of regional rotation has guided the choice, and only one Latin American, Peru's Javier Pérez de Cuéllar, has ever held the post, serving from 1982 to 1991 — which is why Bachelet's backers argued that Latin America was 'in line' this cycle.

In 2016, for the first time, candidates took part in public hearings in the General Assembly, a small step towards the transparent process campaigners have demanded; the straw polls used to whittle down the field remain secret, with each member simply marking a candidate 'encourage', 'discourage' or 'no opinion'.

The UN also faces a money problem: some member states pay their dues late, and the United States is the largest single contributor to the regular budget, which is why Guterres could warn of an 'imminent financial collapse'.

perspectives.description: The straw poll did its job by showing a candidate that her support was evaporating before a bruising public vote, and two women now lead the field — so the glass ceiling may still break this cycle. Grynspan, who runs the UN's trade and development body, and Rodrigues-Birkett both bring deep UN experience and would arrive with wide international backing.

A secret ballot and five national vetoes let a handful of governments decide who is 'electable' before the other 188 members have a say, and Bachelet was pushed out by an unofficial poll rather than a formal vote. The fact that every Secretary-General in 80 years has been a man, and that Latin America's informal 'turn' may now be skipped, shows how much the process still rests on custom and great-power convenience.

Regional rotation is a tradition, not a rule, and the Council has historically favoured consensus figures who will not antagonise the permanent five. The deeper constraint is structural: whoever wins inherits a body that is cash-strapped, veto-bound on Gaza and Ukraine, and judged by member states that increasingly question its value.

Campaigners want candidates to face public hearings and open campaigning, as happened for the first time in 2016, and the coming General Assembly session will test whether that pressure grows. The real question is whether the next Secretary-General can restore trust and finances — and whether the P5 would ever accept someone willing to challenge them.
